paper_title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at https://github.com/ArtKanke/rTaste.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language model agents can now carry out much of the empirical research workflow, from literature search and implementation to running experiments and writing reports (Lu et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2025). Frontier AI labs report that agents write much of their code and support rapidly growing number of experiments (Favaro & Clark, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). risk assessment of agents inside four frontier labs, however, found no evidence that any of them relied on agents to set research agendas or make budget decisions (METR, 2026). The step that has not been delegated is close to what researchers call taste, the judgment of which questions and experiments are worth pursuing before their outcomes are known (Hamming, 1986). In practice this judgment is often exercised through small experiments. researcher tests direction cheaply and lets the result decide whether larger study is needed. Such an experiment is useful only if its outcome is not obvious in advance and the researchers expectation about it is accurate enough to act on. An agent that proposes experiments with predictable outcomes or that is confidently wrong about what its experiments will show spends limited budget poorly even if it runs every experiment correctly. Existing evaluations address parts of this question. Execution benchmarks specify task and measure how well an agent completes it (Chan et al., 2025; Starace et al., 2025). Studies of research ideas often judge proposals before execution, although those judgments can change when the ideas are carried out (Si et al., 2026a). Other work tests whether models can predict outcomes or choose among experiments on given problem (Wen et al., 2025; Foster et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). We examine these judgments for experiments that agents propose from recent paper and compare their expectations with the outcomes of every proposal. We ask what experiments agents propose from new paper, how accurately they predict the outcomes, and how well they choose among their proposals. We give each model recent NLP paper, the seed paper, with its code. sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Research agents and benchmarks. Research agent systems now span the workflow from ideation to written reports (Yamada et al., 2025; Miyai et al., 2026), some organized around persistent tree of hypotheses and isolated executors (Jin et al., 2026). RE-Bench, AIRS-Bench, and DeepRSI give agents task with fixed metric and score the result (Wijk et al., 2025; Lupidi et al., 2026; Rajaghatta et al., 2026). TasteVal, concurrent with our work, measures how efficiently models own experiments reach an experts score on fixed task (Jaffe & Sherburn, 2026). EXP-Bench asks agents to reproduce experiments from published papers (Kon et al., 2026). Other benchmarks give agents research problems drawn from recent or unpublished work (Garikaparthi et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). In each, the problem is given to the agent, whereas our agents choose what to test from seed paper. Studies of such agents report frequent failures to complete experiments, reported results that do not match the underlying code (Chen et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b), and weak judgment about when evidence is sufficient (Kirgis et al., 2026). Evaluating research ideas. second group of work evaluates research ideas directly. Blind comparisons with expert researchers found that large language model ideas were rated more novel than human ideas (Si et al., 2025), and studies of expert preferences found that automated judges reproduce those preferences only partially (Chen et al., 2026) or little better than chance (Baig et al.,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: 2026). Judgments of this kind are made without outcomes. When ideas from the earlier study were executed by researchers, the advantage of the model generated ideas disappeared (Si et al., 2026a). Language models asked to judge the soundness of proposals are also strongly biased toward approval (Ho et al., 2026). Agent generated ideas tend to stay close to their source literature (Tang & Yang, 2026). Other studies judge research foresight against the later literature, asking which directions will be pursued or will gain attention (Li et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). Another study compares models proposed next step in project with the step its authors actually took (Gong et al., 2026). Predicting experimental outcomes. The work closest to ours predicts experimental outcomes before execution. Models can predict which of two published ideas performs better on benchmark (Mule et al., 2026), which of two candidate programs will score higher (Zheng et al., 2026), or the numeric result of an experiment from its description (Park et al., 2025). Recent work also asks models which training recipe will reach the lowest loss (Ren et al., 2026b) and how much change to training or inference recipe will improve benchmark score (Wang et al., 2026). Some register expected outcomes before pilot experiments and run only the best supported hypotheses in full (Ren et al., 2026a), so their expectations about the other hypotheses are never checked at full scale. Others run every candidate, to train model that scores hypotheses (Vasu et al., 2025) or to learn from large batches of executed ideas (Si et al., 2026b). Where calibration has been measured for agents, on coding tasks with clear success criteria, agents are overconfident about their own success (Kaddour et al., 2026; Barkan et al., 2025). Research teams. Several research systems divide the work among specialized agents that generate, critique, and rank hypotheses (Gottweis et al., 2026; Schmidgall et al., 2026), and lead agent coordinating parallel subagents has improved performance on research style information tasks at substantially higher token cost (Hadfield et al., 2025). Studies suggest that such gains depend on the task and on how coordination is organized (Kim et al., 2025) and that when total computation is held equal single agent often matches or exceeds multi agent designs (Tran & Kiela, 2026).

sections.title: 3.1 SEED PAPERS
sections.content: We use seven NLP papers (arXiv cs.CL) with released code, taken from the daily papers list on Hugging Face1 and first made public between 3 August and 24 September 2026. We chose papers this recent so that little follow up work exists for an agent to find and repeat. The selection also excludes work that requires large GPU training runs or models with more than 8B parameters. The full list can be found in Appendix A. Agents receive the papers full text, an image of every page, and read access to its code repository. We did not provide summary, suggested research gap or direction, or hypothesis.

sections.title: 3.2 AGENTS AND HARNESSES
sections.content: We evaluate six models at maximum reasoning effort: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and Muse Spark 1.3.2 Evaluation was conducted between 6 and 8 October 2026. Each model works under two harnesses, so each seed paper has twelve conditions. We refer to GPT-6 Luna and Muse Spark 1.3 as the two smaller models and to the other four as the larger models. The judges (Section 3.3) also run at maximum effort, and the executors, novelty judges, auditors, and reviewers at high effort. single researcher (SR) works in one continuous context from reading the seed paper to committing its forecasts. research team (RT) divides the same work among separate instances of the same model. Two proposers each read the seed paper, search the literature, and draft experiments independently. critic examines the pooled drafts once for scientific validity and for feasibility. 1https://huggingface.co/papers 2A reply cut off at the output limit is requested once more at medium effort. This happened for the lead of the Claude Opus 5.5 team on six of the seven seed papers, so 30 of the 415 registrations were written at medium effort.

sections.title: 3.3 PROTOCOL
sections.content: The agent makes two commitments before any experiment runs (Figure 1). First, it proposes five minimum viable experiments. Each MVE is specified in short registration with hypothesis, its closest prior work, and one registered event: stated statistic passes threshold set in advance. Second, the agent gives each MVE probability that its registered event will occur and ranks the five from most to least worth pursuing. We call the MVE it ranks highest its first choice. The proposing agent knows that all proposed MVEs will run, so its ranking states priority rather than deciding what runs. We also ask each of the six models, as judge in new context, for the same forecasts and ranking. They see the seed paper and the five registrations. We do not provide the code, the agents reasoning or forecasts, or which model proposed the MVEs, and they cannot search. We call the judge from the agents own model its same model judge. We run the MVEs of seed paper only after all twelve conditions have committed. After the experiments are committed and before execution, two novelty judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, use the same literature search tool to label each MVE as equivalent to existing work, close variant, or distinct. An MVE labeled equivalent or close variant still runs. To see whether an MVE is an obvious follow up, we also ask each of the six models, given only the seed paper and no search, to list ten follow up experiments it would propose. The two novelty judges check each MVE against these lists, and we count it as an obvious follow up if either finds it there.

sections.title: 3.4 EXECUTION AND EVALUATION
sections.content: Executors. One of two executors, Claude Opus 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol, implements each MVE in new context. The same two executors serve all six models, so smaller models proposals are not held back by its own implementation. The executor sees the seed paper, its code, and the one MVE it implements. We did not provide the other four MVEs, the ranking, the forecasts, or the name of the model that proposed the MVE. All MVEs of one model on seed paper go to the same executor and the executors alternate across seed papers. Because both executors are among the six models, 58 of the 412 delivered MVEs were implemented by separate instance of the model that proposed them. We run every MVE with the same limits, no matter its rank. The executor works on separate machine with one A100 GPU for at most 45 minutes, may run open models of up to 8B parameters, and may not call hosted models.3 If it refuses or exceeds its limits, the other executor makes one independent attempt. If both fail, the MVE is not delivered. Evaluation. We then delete the results that came with the executors submission and rerun its evaluation on new machine the executor never used. The rerun determines whether the registered event occurred. An MVE is delivered when the rerun ends without error and writes number. The rerun repeats the executors own code, so whether that code is right is left to the auditors. Audits. Three auditors, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Grok 4.7, judge every delivered MVE. Grok 4.7 is not one of the six models we study and does not execute. The auditors see the registration, the executors notes, the output of the rerun, and the files it left. They do not see the seed paper or who proposed or implemented the MVE. Each auditor judges whether the MVE is faithful to its registration and valid and rates its research value from 0 to 3. We take the majority of the three judgments of faithfulness and validity and the median of the three research values. We call an MVE sound when it is faithful and valid, valuable when its research value is 2 or 3 and new when neither novelty judge found close prior work. sections.title: 4 FINDINGS
sections.content: Of the 84 conditions, 83 produced MVEs.4 We make each comparison within seed papers and report its average over the seven seed papers, with 95% confidence interval (CI) computed across them.

sections.title: 4.1 QUALITY OF THE MVES
sections.content: We count an MVE as sound, valuable and new when it meets all three (Section 3.4). Nearly all MVEs were delivered and most were judged sound, so most of those that fall short repeat prior work or have low research value. Because the seed papers are recent, new mostly means not yet published: most MVEs on list of obvious follow ups are also new. The four larger models propose about three such MVEs in five and the two smaller models about one. The gap holds for single researchers and for teams, while the order among the four larger models changes from one seed paper to another. The smaller models MVEs often run as registered but leave the question open. For each sound MVE, the reviewers stated what the evidence says about the hypothesis, and we call the evidence informative when at least two of them read it as for, against, or mixed. MVEs of GPT-6 Luna are sound as often as those of GPT-6.1 Sol, but their evidence is informative about half as often (38% against 74%), and that of Muse Spark 1.3 is similar  (Table 1)  .

sections.title: 4.3 REGISTERED EVENTS AND EVIDENCE
sections.content: Each registration commits the agent to one registered event before the MVE runs and it is natural to read the event as the success of the experiment. For each sound MVE, we compare whether the event occurred with the reviewers reading of the evidence. Whether the event occurs depends on how the agent defines it. In most of their MVEs, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol compare bound of confidence interval with the threshold, rather than point estimate  (Table 7)  , and the other four models rarely do. The events of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol occur in 25% of their sound MVEs, compared with 52% for Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5  (Table 1)  . On one seed paper (Liang et al., 2026), four conditions tested whether models own prediction errors harm decoding more than random errors of the same size, and all three reviewers read all four results as support for it. Three of the conditions had set the threshold at difference of 5 percentage points and their events occurred. The fourth had set it at 8 points, and its event did not. When the registered event does not occur, the evidence is often still informative. The reviewers judged the evidence informative for 50% of the sound MVEs whose event did not occur, mostly as evidence against the hypothesis. In the other direction, they judged the evidence inconclusive for 20% of the sound MVEs whose event occurred.

sections.title: 4.4 FORECASTS
sections.content: We next ask whether the agent that designed an MVE forecasts its registered event better than an outside reader. The outside reader is the same model judge, which sees only the seed paper and the five registrations. The agents own reading and search did not measurably improve its forecasts over this readers: the difference between their Brier scores (lower is better) is 0.006, with 95% CI from 0.021 to 0.009  (Table 3)  . Both forecasts are more accurate than base rate that gives every MVE the event rate of the other six seed papers (Brier score 0.240), and the mean of the six judges probabilities is more accurate than the agent (0.179 against 0.192). The agent has seen more than its registrations state, but it is not shown to know more about its events than its registrations tell reader. The agents are also not uniformly overconfident: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna and Muse Spark 1.3 state higher probabilities than the rates at which their events occur, while Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 state lower ones.

sections.title: 4.5 FIRST CHOICES
sections.content: The agents first choice is the auditors most valued MVE in 38% of conditions, where random pick gives 20%. The MVE that the agent wrote first and the same model judges first choice are the most valued about as often, and we find no evidence that the agents first choice beats either: its advantage over the MVE written first is 3 percentage points (95% CI 8 to 15). The first choice is also sound, valuable and new no more often than random pick. Agents register their obvious experiments first: the MVE written first is on list of obvious follow ups in 61% of conditions, against 35% for the fifth. The agents then rank largely in the order in which they wrote them, and their first choice is the MVE they wrote first in 47% of conditions, where 20% would be expected if order did not matter. The event of the first choice occurs in 47% of conditions and that of the last choice in 29%, so the first choice is often an experiment likely to come out as registered. The auditors also rank sound MVEs whose event occurred higher, mostly because these MVEs give clearer evidence. The judges rank in the same way: they too put the MVE written first on top in 39% of conditions on average. They and the auditors also rank obvious follow ups higher, and an agents ranking agrees more with the same model judge and with other judges from the same provider than with judges from other providers. On average, judges first choice is an MVE beyond the paper and non obvious less often than random pick would be, while the agents own first choice is one about as often.

sections.title: 4.7 EXECUTION AND RESOURCES
sections.content: A condition cost $15.31 on average for single researcher and $23.93 for team, counting the agents model calls and the implementation and rerun of its five MVEs  (Table 1)  . Per $100, single researchers produced 13 sound, valuable and new MVEs and teams 11, and GPT-6.1 Sol produced the most. The cost of proposing differs about hundredfold between models, from GPT-6 Luna to Claude Fable 5.1, while the cost of implementing and rerunning an MVE differs about twofold, since the same two executors served every model. Without the requirement of novelty, team of GPT-6 Luna produced as many sound and valuable MVEs per $100 as GPT-6.1 Sol, but about half as many beyond the paper and non obvious, where GPT-6.1 Sol produced the most. The executors delivered 397 of the 415 MVEs on their first attempt, and the limits were rarely reached: the median implementation took 12 minutes, well within its limits (Appendix A.3). The agents reached their tool call limit in 5% of conditions. The MVEs of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 take more than twice as much GPU time to implement as those of GPT-6 Astra and GPT6.1 Sol  (Table 4)  . The auditors judge 18% of the MVEs implemented by the Claude Opus 5.5 executor not sound, compared with 3% of those implemented by the GPT-6.1 Sol executor, while the evidence is informative equally often under both.

sections.title: 5 DISCUSSION
sections.content: We began this study to see how many good small experiments frontier models can propose when recent paper is their source of inspiration. By good MVE we mean one that is small and not obvious and that opens direction worth larger study. Most of the experiments were sound, but most either tested the seed paper itself or extended it in way that many researchers would propose, and few opened new direction. Current agents appear better suited to examining paper and taking its obvious next steps than to moving beyond it. That is useful in itself, since new papers claims can be checked under controls and stricter measurements for few dollars each, but it is different capability from proposing new research, and evaluations of research agents should measure the two separately. The models differ less in how often their experiments are sound than in what kind of experiment they propose. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol more often go beyond the paper with an experiment that is not obvious and register stricter tests, which pass less often. Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 stay closer to the paper and register tests that pass more often. The experiments of the two smaller models more often leave the question open. Choosing model is therefore also choosing

Because the price of proposing differs far more between models than the cost of running an MVE, small model working as team with capable executor yields about as many sound and valuable experiments per dollar as the most efficient large model, though fewer beyond the paper. In our study every experiment ran with the same limits, so the agents rankings stated priorities and did not decide what would be implemented. Those rankings followed the order in which the agents wrote their MVEs and favored the ones likely to pass. natural next study gives an agent fixed research budget to allocate among its own MVEs and to revise after the first results, and asks whether the budget goes to the MVEs that turn out sound, valuable and non obvious. The same budget given to human researchers would show how their allocations compare and provide human baseline. This would extend the evaluation from what an agent proposes and expects to how it spends limited budget, the decision in which researchers exercise their taste.

sections.title: 6 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: All labels in this study come from models, so we lack human baseline. The auditors judged soundness and value after seeing the outcomes and two of the three are models we also evaluate and use as executors. Every MVE was attempted regardless of its rank, so the ranking did not decide what ran. An agent whose ranking decides what runs may rank with more reasoning. Each registration had to be complete enough for separate executor, so part of the forecasting result may be built into the design. Each condition ran once, so we have no measure of how much result would change on second run.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied whether research agents can evaluate and predict the outcomes of their own experiments before they are run. Given recent NLP paper, six frontier models proposed small experiments, forecast whether the result of each would pass threshold they set and ranked them. separate executor attempted every proposed experiment. We find that the agents propose experiments that are often sound, valuable and new. sections.content: You are the engineer who implements one registered experiment. Implement it as registered: keep its hypothesis, method, registered event, controls and evaluation. Do not change the experiment to make it easier or to make the event occur. They are not results of the evaluation, and the engineers notes may also quote those earlier runs. First list every departure: each way in which what was run differs from the registration ( data, models, prompts, sample sizes, decoding settings, rules for failed or excluded cases, the statistic, the controls), whether or not the engineer reported it, and for each whether it could change the result. Then judge three things. 1. Fidelity to the registration. "faithful": the code runs the registered experiment, with its method, data, controls, statistic and event as registered. These do not make it unfaithful: choice the registration leaves open, change needed for the registered experiment to run at all (for example larger context window so that the registered inputs fit), and departure that did not plausibly change the reported value. "unfaithful": at least one departure plausibly changed the reported value or changes the question, for example prompt, sample, model or decoding setting other than the registered one, rule for failed or excluded cases that the registration does not contain and that affected the value, or change the registration forbids. "unknown": the evidence does not let you tell. null result or failed hypothesis is not fidelity defect, and successful run alone does not establish fidelity. 2. Validity of the evidence. "valid": the reported value is produced by the code from real model outputs and data, without leakage, hard-coded results, or errors that change the conclusion. "invalid": otherwise. "unknown": you cannot tell. 3. Research value, from 0 to 3: 0: established non-delivery, or invalid or unsupported evidence; 1: valid but weak or uninformative evidence; 2: meaningful, credible, supported finding; 3: particularly strong and consequential evidence with adequate controls and precision. meaningful, well-supported null finding can receive 2 or 3. Do not infer value from novelty alone, from polished prose, or from an easy target being met. Give null if you cannot judge. You have no tools: everything you can look at is in this message. Its figures are not shown and its tables are broken into lines. <seed_paper id="$arxiv_id"> $paper </seed_paper> You review one small experiment that was planned after this paper and then built and run. After the questions below you get its written plan (a "registration"), the notes of the engineer who built it, the output of its evaluation and the files the evaluation left. The plans writer had read this paper, could also read the papers code and data and search the literature, and was told to choose their own question and method. The plan was written before anything was run. Every such plan had the same limits: one GPU for at most 45 minutes , and open models of 8B parameters or fewer. So it is first small test. separate engineer model then built the experiment from the paper and the registration, and the engineers evaluation command was run once more on fresh machine. You are not told which models wrote the plan or built the experiment. You give eleven answers: seven about the idea, then four about what came out. The answers are used to count kinds of experiment, so choose the line that fits, not the one that sounds best. For each answer, write the reason in one sentence first, then the answer. PART ONE: THE IDEA The first seven answers are about the plan as it was written. Give them as you would have before the run: how the run came out does not make an idea more or less obvious, or its question more or less worth asking.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Four fields of the plan are the writers own account of it: seed_connection, contribution, closest_work and full_scale_study. They say how the writer sees the link to the paper, what is new, and what larger study could follow. They are claims, not facts. Use them for one answer only, misreads_paper, where every statement the plan makes about the paper is checked against the paper. Give every other answer as you would if these four fields were empty. These must not move any of the seven answers: - how long, detailed or polished the text is, or how many controls it lists; - whether you think the hypothesis is true, or how the run came out; - that the experiment is small, or uses smaller model or fewer examples than the paper because of the limits; - whether this exact experiment has been published. what_it_asks. One sentence of your own, taken from the hypothesis, the method and the event: what is compared with what, on what, to learn what. Leave out sample sizes, controls, statistics and thresholds. in_the_paper. Look through the whole paper, appendix included. - "reported": the paper reports this experiment, or number or comparison that already answers its hypothesis by the same kind of measurement. - "named": the paper does not report it, and says in its own words that this question is left undone: as future work, as limitation, or as an open question. - "neither": anything else. sentence that only describes what the paper did, admits weakness, explains result without measuring it, or calls for more work in general, is not "named". For "reported" or "named", copy into "quote" the passage of the paper that shows it: between 5 and 40 words in row, exactly as printed, with nothing left out. Running prose and prompt listings count; tables and formulas do not. If you cannot point to such passage, the answer is "neither" and "quote" is null. relation. What is the hypothesis about? Decide by what the experiment tests and uses, not by its controls or side analyses, and not by whether the text mentions the paper. The hypothesis is about the papers own claims or results: - "reruns": that reported result comes out again. - "checks": that claim or result the paper states holds up, or fails, under control, baseline, test for confound or stricter measurement. - "varies": that result of the paper holds, or fails, on another model, dataset or language, with the papers method unchanged. - "explains": why reported result arises. Choose this only when the result is taken as real; if the hypothesis is that the result comes from confound or an artifact, choose " checks". The hypothesis is about something the paper does not claim or report: - "builds on": the papers method, data, benchmark or result is working part of the experiment, and is changed, extended or put to use the paper does not make of it. test of property or side effect of the papers method that the paper makes no claim about belongs here: the papers claims stand whichever way it comes out. - "new direction": the experiment uses none of these. The paper only prompted the question. If two lines fit, choose the one that fits the hypothesis better. obvious. Picture ten researchers who work in this papers area and know its literature. Each has just read the paper and writes down the ten follow-up experiments that come to mind first. On how many of the ten lists would the idea of this experiment appear? The idea is the question and the main comparison in your what_it_asks sentence, without the test bed and the measurement. list contains the idea if it has an experiment that asks the same question with the same main comparison. list that has only the broader worry does not. Ask what they would write before seeing this plan, not whether the idea looks natural once read . - "most": six or more lists. - "some": three to five. - "few": one or two. - "none": no list. These researchers know the standard techniques of the area. That makes an idea built on one of them available to them; still count how many would put it among their first ten. An elaborate design, an invented test bed, or the lack of published version does not make an idea less obvious. Being simple to run, or looking likely to work, does not make it more obvious. check of the paper can be an idea few would list. step away from the paper can be one most would list. who_would_care. Suppose the question behind this experiment, at the scope its hypothesis states, were followed through to clear answer. Of the outcomes it could have, take the one that would change more. Who would then do or believe something different? - "nobody". - "a few groups": only people who work with the one method, benchmark or system the experiment is about. - "one topic": people across research topic would change how they do their own work, whatever method or benchmark they use. - "several topics": people across several topics; common practice or belief would change. Count the people who would act on the answer. question is not wide because it mentions large field. How close the question is to the paper does not matter here.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: misreads_paper. Does the plan depend on statement about the paper (what it did, found or claimed) that the papers text shows to be false? Look at every field, the writers own account included. - "yes": copy into "quote" the passage of the paper that shows it, by the same rule as above . If you cannot point to such passage, the answer is "no" and "quote" is null. - "no". - "nothing stated": the plan states nothing about the paper that can be checked against its text. Doubting or testing claim of the paper is not misreading. Repeating the papers own summary of itself is not one either. The writer could see the papers code and data and you cannot: file name, released model or setting that the papers text does not mention is not an error, and where the plan follows the code and the code differs from the text, that is not an error. answerable. As it was designed, could this experiment answer the question in your what_it_asks sentence? Go by everything the plan says it will report, not only its one registered number. - "yes": clear result either way would bear on the question. - "only if": the result can be read only if something else holds first, which the design cannot make sure of: for example that an effect of the paper appears at this small scale, that model trained in the experiment learns what it is trained for, or that measurement or control behaves as it should. This is the answer whether or not the plan checks that thing itself. Name the one such thing that matters most in "needs", in few words. - "no": the design cannot answer the question as written, for example because the comparison leaves out what it claims to test, or no number it could produce could be read. Judge the design as written, not by whether the run happened to work. Do not judge whether the hypothesis is likely to be true. Whether this many cases can give clear result is not asked here: small size alone is not reason for "no", and "the effect may be too small to see" is not reason for "only if". PART TWO: WHAT CAME OUT The last four answers are about the run. good plan can give run that tells nothing, and weak plan run that tells something. The engineers notes are the engineers own account: go by the numbers in the evaluation output and the files. Numbers the evaluation computed count, including checks the engineer added; where you can, check them against the raw outputs shown. Files marked "submitted, not written by the evaluation" came with the engineers submission, for example logs and results of the engineers own earlier runs. They are not results of the evaluation, and the engineers notes may also quote those earlier runs. The plan registered an event: one number set against one bar. The output says whether it occurred. None of the four answers is that. Writers set bars differently: point value, confidence bound, or number written into the hypothesis. So missed bar can come with clear evidence and met bar with none. Look at how large the measured effect is and how sure the run is of it, and judge the same way whichever kind of bar the plan used. Others have checked whether the code follows the plan. You need not list departures. Take the experiment as it was run. what_came_out. One sentence with the numbers of the main comparison, how sure the run is of them (its interval if it gives one, otherwise the number of cases and repetitions), and the model and data. Do not say here whether the event occurred. prerequisite. test can rest on something that must hold before its main comparison can be read: that an effect of the paper appears at this scale, that model trained in the experiment learned what it was trained for, or that measurement or control behaved as it should. It is something other than the hypothesis itself. If you named such thing in " needs", look at it first; then look for any other. - "held": as far as the run shows, nothing of this kind failed, or there was no such thing. - "failed": one such thing did not hold, or did not pass the plans own check for it, so the main comparison cannot be read. Name it in "which". - "cannot tell": the run does not show whether such thing held. Name it in "which". With "failed" or "cannot tell", set "named_before" to true if "which" is what you named in " needs", otherwise false. fault that the run itself shows did not change the main comparison is not failure. Too few cases or too much noise is not one either; that belongs under "evidence". evidence. What does the run say about the plans hypothesis? number inside the hypothesis is the plans bar. Do not answer by which side of it the result fell: clear effect in the claimed direction, somewhat smaller than that number, is evidence for. If the hypothesis claims that something makes no difference or does not hold up, run that clearly shows this is evidence for. - "for": the run shows what the hypothesis claims, and noise alone would not explain it. - "against": the run could have shown what the hypothesis claims and clearly shows otherwise . The change being tested was really applied and the measurement was not stuck at its floor or ceiling. For claimed effect, the measured effect is near zero or reversed and an effect large enough to matter is ruled out. - "mixed": the run is sure of two things that point opposite ways, for example an effect on one model and its reverse on another, or gain with measured loss.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: - "inconclusive": the run does not tell either way: prerequisite failed, or the uncertainty leaves room both for no effect and for an effect large enough to matter. - "cannot judge": the numbers needed are not in what you are shown, or the code shows they do not measure what the plan describes. If "prerequisite" is "failed", the answer is "inconclusive". If the hypothesis has two parts and one could not be tested, the answer is "inconclusive", not "mixed". If the run gives no interval, judge from the number of cases and repetitions and say so. next_step. An experiment of this kind is cheap first test of whether question deserves larger study. The question is the one in your what_it_asks sentence. Going only by what this run shows, what should careful researcher do next about it? - "larger study": the run justifies study of many times its cost on the same question. It need not be the study in the plans last field, and the evidence may be for or against the hypothesis. - "one more experiment": the run answered its own question, and one gap must be closed by further small experiment before choosing between larger study and stop. Name the experiment in "what". - "repair": the run did not answer its own question and shows why. The same question must be asked again with the fault removed. Name the fault and the fix in "what". Too few cases is such fault. - "stop": the run justifies spending no more on this question, because (a) the idea was credibly shown not to work, or (b) something the whole question depends on was credibly shown not to hold, or (c) the question is settled and larger study would add nothing that matters. Give the letter in "what". - "no decision": the run did not answer its own question and does not show what to fix. justified stop is as good an answer as justified larger study, and neither follows from the bar. If "evidence" is "inconclusive" or "cannot judge", the answer is "repair", "no decision", or "stop" on ground (b). You have no tools: everything you can look at is in this message.
